query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy, accelerated coupled degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature arises because the galvanic coupling between the softer FCC matrix and the harder intermetallic (σ) phases creates localized anodic sites. This leads to localized corrosion that disrupts the protective oxide film and weakens the matrix, thereby enhancing wear damage.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic HEA featuring an FCC matrix interspersed with discrete intermetallic (σ) phases.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear (such as sliding or reciprocating wear) and a corrosive medium (e.g., chloride‐containing solution) at elevated temperatures.
generation.conditions: Testing is conducted at elevated temperatures (approximately 400–600 °C) in a corrosive environment (for example, 3.5 wt.% NaCl or a similarly aggressive chloride/acidic solution) under conditions that promote both wear and corrosion.
generation.structural_mediator: The interphase boundaries between the FCC matrix and the σ-phase establish micro-galvanic cells due to differences in electrochemical potential.
generation.mechanism: The micro-galvanic cells accelerate localized corrosion at the phase boundaries. Localized breakdown of the protective oxide layer allows wear to more easily remove material, which further exposes fresh substrate to corrosion. This synergistic interaction between wear-induced oxide film disruption and accelerated corrosion leads to an overall increase in the degradation rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a matched baseline (a single-phase HEA or separate isolated wear or corrosion tests), the alloy will exhibit increased total degradation characterized by a higher mass loss, elevated wear rates, and higher corrosion current densities. Specifically, the wear damage will be exacerbated by corrosion-induced weakening of the matrix, while corrosion itself is accelerated by the disruption of passivating films from mechanical wear.
generation.baseline: A comparable material with a homogenized, single-phase microstructure or separate tests under only wear or only corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted synergistic degradation behavior is expected under elevated temperature and corrosive conditions that allow for both phase-specific galvanic interactions and oxide instability. At room temperature or in inert environments where oxide formation or galvanic differences are minimized, the effect is not expected to be pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative mechanism is supported by evidence from multiphase HEA coatings showing galvanic corrosion between FCC and σ phases, the quantitative magnitude of the effect may vary with the precise phase distribution and oxide stability. There is uncertainty in the exact percentage increase in degradation, which will depend on the alloy’s microstructural details and testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: (a) the multi-phase eutectic HEA with both FCC and σ phases, and (b) a matched alloy engineered to have a single-phase homogeneous microstructure. Subject both to simultaneous wear and corrosion testing at elevated temperature under identical conditions, as well as to isolated wear-only and corrosion-only tests.
measurements: Wear rate via profilometry or volume loss measurements
Corrosion current density using electrochemical techniques (potentiodynamic polarization)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess oxide layer stability
Microstructural and surface chemistry analysis (SEM, EDS) to assess localized corrosion at phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multi-phase alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in combined degradation (both wear and corrosion) relative to the single-phase alloy under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions, or if altering the phase structure to alter galvanic coupling does not correlate with changes in degradation rates, then the hypothesis that galvanic interactions between dissimilar phases are the primary driver for the accelerated degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power
